request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a gradual increase in abdominal girth over the past two years, along with abdominal distension and intermittent nausea for the past six months. The patient also experienced repeated intractable hiccups for two months, leading to the hospital admission. Physical examination revealed a longitudinal surgical scar on the upper abdomen and a swelling of the mass on the left side of the abdomen.

Further diagnostic investigations were performed, including ultrasonography, computerized tomography (CT), and an isotope kidney scan. These tests revealed the presence of a massive hypoechoic lesion occupying almost the entire abdomen, exerting pressure on the stomach, liver, pancreas, and spleen. Adhesion between the kidney and surrounding organs was evident during the laparoscopy and open simple nephrectomy procedure.

About 7.5 liters of hydronephrosis fluid were drained, and the left kidney and upper ureter were successfully removed, resulting in the disappearance of long-lasting hiccups and improvement of the patient's appetite and overall health. After the operation, the patient was observed for six months, during which there was no recurrence of the hiccups.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was discharged with instructions to follow a proper diet and continue with regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare professional.

Dictated by: [Redacted]
Signed electronically by: [Redacted]

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: N13**

The principal diagnosis is massive left hydronephrosis, which the episode was built around. It caused the abdominal distension and mass, and it was treated by draining about 7.5 L of fluid and performing a left nephrectomy. Hydronephrosis indexes to the obstructive and reflux uropathy category (N13) in ICD-10-AM. The hiccups and nausea were symptoms of the mass effect, not the principal diagnosis.

The record does not name the underlying cause of the obstruction or state whether a neoplasm was confirmed, and the diagnosis section is withheld. If the pathology showed a renal neoplasm as the cause, the coding would change, so this answer depends on the withheld diagnosis.
